entries.16acc7e8f11003d1b22131257d610debb9d2c9f7: <div sID="gen30728" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="Rom.10" sID="Rom.10"/> <div eID="gen30728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30729" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30730" type="x-p"/> The dissolving of the peculiar church-state of the Jews, and the rejection of that polity by the repealing of their ceremonial law, the vacating of all the institutions of it, the abolishing of their priesthood, the burning of their temple, and the taking away of their place and nation, and in their room the substituting and erecting of a catholic church-state among the Gentile nations, though to us, now that these things have long since been done and completed, they may seem no great matter, yet to those who lived when they were doing, who knew how high the Jews had stood in God's favour, and how deplorable the condition of the Gentile world had been for many ages, it appeared very great and marvellous, and a mystery hard to be understood. The apostle, in this chapter, as in the foregoing and that which follows, is explaining and proving it; but with several very useful digressions, which a little interrupt the thread of his discourse. To two great truths I would reduce this chapter:—I. That there is a great difference between the righteousness of the law, which the unbelieving Jews were wedded to, and the righteousness of faith offered in the gospel, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.1-Rom.10.11">ver. 1-11</reference>. II. That there is no difference between Jews and Gentiles; but, in point of justification and acceptance with God, the gospel sets them both upon the same level, <reference osisRef="Rom.12">ver. 12 to the end</reference>.
entries.1cf348806c5fc6fc67a12b54a10180eee770f3f1: <div eID="gen30730" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30729" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Paul's Discourse of Righteousness; The Method of Salvation. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 58.)</title> <div sID="gen30731" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Brethren, my heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved. <hi type="super">2</hi> For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge. <hi type="super">3</hi> For they being ignorant of God's righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God. <hi type="super">4</hi> For Christ <hi type="italic">is</hi> the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth. <hi type="super">5</hi> For Moses describeth the righteousness which is of the law, That the man which doeth those things shall live by them. <hi type="super">6</hi> But the righteousness which is of faith speaketh on this wise, Say not in thine heart, Who shall ascend into heaven? (that is, to bring Christ down <hi type="italic">from above:</hi>) 7 Or, Who shall descend into the deep? (that is, to bring up Christ again from the dead.) <hi type="super">8</hi> But what saith it? The word is nigh thee, <hi type="italic">even</hi> in thy mouth, and in thy heart: that is, the word of faith, which we preach; <hi type="super">9</hi> That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved. 10 For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. <hi type="super">11</hi> For the scripture saith, Whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed. <div eID="gen30731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30732" type="x-p"/> The scope of the apostle in this part of the chapter is to show the vast difference between the righteousness of the law and the righteousness of faith, and the great pre-eminence of the righteousness of faith above that of the law; that he might induce and persuade the Jews to believe in Christ, aggravate the folly and sin of those that refused, and justify God in the rejection of such refusers. <div eID="gen30732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30733" type="x-p"/> I. Paul here professes his good affection to the Jews, with the reason of it (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.1-Rom.10.2">v. 1, 2</reference>), where he gives them a good wish, and a good witness. <div eID="gen30733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30734" type="x-p"/> 1. A good wish (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.1">v. 1</reference>), a wish that they might be saved—saved from the temporal ruin and destruction that were coming upon them—saved from the wrath to come, eternal wrath, which was hanging over their heads. It is implied in this wish that they might be convinced and converted; he could not pray in faith that they might be saved in their unbelief. Though Paul preached against them, yet he prayed for them. Herein he was merciful, as God is, who is <hi type="italic">not willing that any should perish</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.9">2 Pet. iii. 9</reference>), desires not the death of sinners. It is our duty truly and earnestly to desire the salvation of our own. This, he says, was <hi type="italic">his heart's desire and prayer,</hi> which intimates, (1.) The strength and sincerity of his desire. It was <hi type="italic">his heart's desire;</hi> it was not a formal compliment, as good wishes are with many from the teeth outward, but a real desire. This it was before it was his prayer. The soul of prayer is the heart's desire. Cold desires do but beg denials; we must even breathe out our souls in every prayer. (2.) The offering up of this desire to God. It was not only his heart's desire, but it was his prayer. There may be desires in the heart, and yet no prayer, unless those desires be presented to God. Wishing and woulding, if that be all, are not praying. <div eID="gen30734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30735" type="x-p"/> 2. A good witness, as a reason of his good wish (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">I bear them record that they have a zeal of God.</hi> The unbelieving Jews were the most bitter enemies Paul had in the world, and yet Paul gives them as good a character as the truth would bear. We should say the best we can even of our worst enemies; this is blessing those that curse us. Charity teaches us to have the best opinion of persons, and to put the best construction upon words and actions, that they will bear. We should take notice of that which is commendable even in bad people. <hi type="italic">They have a zeal of God.</hi> Their opposition to the gospel is from a principle of respect to the law, which they know to have come from God. There is such a thing as a blind misguided zeal: such was that of the Jews, who, when they hated Christ's people and ministers, and cast them out, said, <hi type="italic">Let the Lord be glorified</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.5">Isa. lxvi. 5</reference>); nay, they killed them, and thought they did God good service, <reference osisRef="John.16.2">John xvi. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen30735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30736" type="x-p"/> II. He here shows the fatal mistake that the unbelieving Jews were guilty of, which was their ruin. Their zeal was <hi type="italic">not according to knowledge.</hi> It is true God gave them that law for which they were so zealous; but they might have known that, by the appearance of the promised Messiah, an end was put to it. He introduced a new religion and way of worship, to which the former must give place. He proved himself the Son of God, gave the most convincing evidence that could be of his being the Messiah; and yet they did not know and would not own him, but shut their eyes against the clear light, so that their zeal for the law was blind. This he shows further, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.3">v. 3</reference>, where we may observe, <div eID="gen30736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30737" type="x-p"/> 1. The nature of their unbelief. They <hi type="italic">have not submitted themselves to the righteousness of God,</hi> that is, they have not yielded to gospel-terms, nor accepted the tender of justification by faith in Christ, which is made in the gospel. Unbelief is a non-submission to the righteousness of God, standing it out against the gospel proclamation of indemnity. <hi type="italic">Have not submitted.</hi> In true faith, there is need of a great deal of submission; therefore the first lesson Christ teaches is to deny ourselves. It is a great piece of condescension for a proud heart to be content to be beholden to free grace; we are loth to sue <hi type="italic">sub forma pauperis—as paupers.</hi> <div eID="gen30737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30738" type="x-p"/> 2. The causes of their unbelief, and these are two:—(1.) Ignorance of God's righteousness. They did not understand, and believe, and consider, the strict justice of God, in hating and punishing sin, and demanding satisfaction, did not consider what need we have of a righteousness wherein to appear before him; if they had, they would never have stood out against the gospel offer, nor expected justification by their own works, as if they could satisfy God's justice. Or, being ignorant of God's way of justification, which he has now appointed and revealed by Jesus Christ. They did not know it, because they would not; they shut their eyes against the discoveries of it, and love darkness rather. (2.) A proud conceit of their own righteousness: <hi type="italic">Going about to establish their own</hi>—a righteousness of their own devising, and of their own working out, by the merit of their works, and by their observance of the ceremonial law. They thought they needed not to be beholden to the merit of Christ, and therefore depended upon their own performances as sufficient to make up a righteousness wherein to appear before God. They could not with Paul disclaim a dependence upon this (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.9">Phil. iii. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">Not having my own righteousness.</hi> See an instance of this pride in the Pharisee, <reference osisRef="Luke.18.10-Luke.18.11">Luke xviii. 10, 11</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Rom.10.14">v. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen30738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30739" type="x-p"/> III. He here shows the folly of that mistake, and what an unreasonable thing it was for them to be seeking justification by the works of the law, now that Christ had come, and had brought in an everlasting righteousness; considering, <div eID="gen30739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30740" type="x-p"/> 1. The subserviency of the law to the gospel (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Christ is the end of the law for righteousness.</hi> The design of the law was to lead people to Christ. The moral law was but for the searching of the wound, the ceremonial law for the shadowing forth of the remedy; but Christ is the end of both. See <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.7">2 Cor. iii. 7, and compare Gal. iii. 23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.23-Gal.3.24">24</reference>. The use of the law was to direct people for righteousness to Christ. (1.) Christ is the end of the ceremonial law; he is the period of it, because he is the perfection of it. When the substance comes, the shadow is gone. The sacrifices, and offerings, and purifications appointed under the Old Testament, prefigured Christ, and pointed at him; and their inability to take away sin discovered the necessity of a sacrifice that should, by being once offered, take away sin. (2.) Christ is the end of the moral law in that he did what the law could not do (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.3">ch. viii. 3</reference>), and secured the great end of it. The end of the law was to bring men to perfect obedience, and so to obtain justification. This is now become impossible, by reason of the power of sin and the corruption of nature; but Christ is the end of the law. The law is not destroyed, nor the intention of the lawgiver frustrated, but, full satisfaction being made by the death of Christ for our breach of the law, the end is attained, and we are put in another way of justification. Christ is thus the end of the law for righteousness, that is, for justification; but it is only to <hi type="italic">every one that believeth.</hi> Upon our believing, that is, our humble consent to the terms of the gospel, we become interested in Christ's satisfaction, and so are justified through the redemption that is in Jesus. <div eID="gen30740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30741" type="x-p"/> 2. The excellency of the gospel above the law. This he proves by showing the different constitution of these two. <div eID="gen30741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30742" type="x-p"/> (1.) What is the righteousness which is of the law? This he shows, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.5">v. 5</reference>. The tenour of it is, <hi type="italic">Do, and live.</hi> Though it directs us to a better and more effectual righteousness in Christ, yet in itself, considered as a law abstracted from its respect to Christ and the gospel (for so the unbelieving Jews embraced and retained it), it owneth nothing as a righteousness sufficient to justify a man but that of perfect obedience. For this he quotes that scripture (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.5">Lev. xviii. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">You shall therefore keep my statutes and my judgments, which if a man do, he shall live in them.</hi> To this he refers likewise, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.12">Gal. iii. 12</reference>, <hi type="italic">The man that doeth them, shall live in them. Live,</hi> that is, be happy, not only in the land of Canaan, but in heaven, of which Canaan was a type and figure. The doing supposed must be perfect and sinless, without the least breach or violation. The law which was given upon Mount Sinai, though it was not a pure covenant of works (for who then could be saved under that dispensation?) yet, that is might be the more effectual to drive people to Christ and to make the covenant of grace welcome, it had a very great mixture of the strictness and terror of the covenant of works. Now, was it not extreme folly in the Jews to adhere so closely to this way of justification and salvation, which was in itself so hard, and by the corruption of nature now become impossible, when there was a new and a living way opened? <div eID="gen30742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30743" type="x-p"/> (2.) What is that righteousness which is of faith, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.6">v. 6</reference>, &c. This he describes in the words of Moses, in Deuteronomy, in the <hi type="italic">second law</hi> (so Deuteronomy signifies), where there was a much clearer revelation of Christ and the gospel than there was in the first giving of the law: he quotes it from <reference osisRef="Deut.30.11-Deut.30.14">Deut. xxx. 11-14</reference>, and shows, <div eID="gen30743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30744" type="x-p"/> [1.] That it is not at all hard or difficult. The way of justification and salvation has in it no such depths or knots as may discourage us, no insuperable difficulties attending it; but, as was foretold, it is a high-way, <reference osisRef="Isa.35.8">Isa. xxxv. 8</reference>. We are not put to climb for it—it is not in heaven; we are not put to dive for it—it is not in the deep. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> We need not go to heaven, to search the records there, or to enquire into the secrets of the divine counsel. It is true Christ is in heaven; but we may be justified and saved without going thither, to fetch him thence, or sending a special messenger to him. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> We need not go to the deep, to fetch Christ out of the grave, or from the state of the dead: <hi type="italic">Into the deep, to bring up Christ from the dead.</hi> This plainly shows that Christ's descent into the <hi type="italic">deep,</hi> or into <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hades,</hi></hi> was no more than his going into the state of the dead, in allusion to Jonah. It is true that Christ was in the grave, and it is as true that he is now in heaven; but we need not perplex and puzzle ourselves with fancied difficulties, nor must we create to ourselves such gross and carnal ideas of these things as if the method of salvation were impracticable, and the design of the revelation were only to amuse us. No, salvation is not put at so vast a distance from us. <div eID="gen30744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30745" type="x-p"/> [2.] But it is very plain and easy: <hi type="italic">The word is nigh thee.</hi> When we speak of looking upon Christ, and receiving Christ, and feeding upon Christ, it is not Christ in heaven, nor Christ in the deep, that we mean; but Christ in the promise, Christ exhibited to us, and offered, in the word. Christ is nigh thee, for the word is nigh thee: nigh thee indeed: it is <hi type="italic">in thy mouth, and in thy heart;</hi> there is no difficulty in understanding, believing, and owning it. The work thou hast to do lies within thee: <hi type="italic">the kingdom of God is within you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.17.21">Luke xvii. 21</reference>. Thence thou must fetch thy evidences, not out of the records of heaven. <hi type="italic">It is,</hi> that is, it is promised that it shall be, <hi type="italic">in thy mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.21">Isa. lix. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">and in thy heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.31.33">Jer. xxxi. 33</reference>. All that which is done for us is already done to our hands. Christ is come down from heaven; we need not go to fetch him. He is come up from the deep; we need not perplex ourselves how to bring him up. There is nothing now to be done, but a work in us; this must be our care, to look to our heart and mouth. Those that were under the law were to do all themselves, <hi type="italic">Do this, and live;</hi> but the gospel discovers the greatest part of the work done already, and what remains cut short in righteousness, salvation offered upon very plain and easy terms, brought to our door, as it were, in the word which is nigh us. It is in our mouth—we are reading it daily; it is in our heart—we are, or should be, thinking of it daily. Even <hi type="italic">the word of faith;</hi> the gospel and the promise of it, called the word of faith because it is the object of faith about which it is conversant, the word which we believe;—because it is the precept of faith, commanding it, and making it the great condition of justification;—and because it is the ordinary means by which faith is wrought and conveyed. Now what is this word of faith? We have the tenour of it, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.9-Rom.10.10">v. 9, 10</reference>, the sum of the gospel, which is plain and easy enough. Observe, <div eID="gen30745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30746" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> What is promised to us: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt be saved.</hi> It is salvation that the gospel exhibits and tenders—saved from guilt and wrath, with the salvation of the soul, an eternal salvation, which Christ is the author of, a Saviour to the uttermost. <div eID="gen30746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30747" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Upon what terms. <div eID="gen30747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30748" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> Two things are required as conditions of salvation:—(<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) <hi type="italic">Confessing the Lord Jesus</hi>—openly professing relation to him and dependence on him, as our prince and Saviour, owning Christianity in the face of all the allurements and affrightments of this world, standing by him in all weathers. Our Lord Jesus lays a great stress upon this confessing of him before men; see <reference osisRef="Matt.10.32-Matt.10.33">Matt. x. 32, 33</reference>. It is the product of many graces, evinces a great deal of self-denial, love to Christ, contempt of the world, a mighty courage and resolution. It was a very great thing, especially, when the profession of Christ or Christianity hazarded estate, honour, preferment, liberty, life, and all that is dear in this world, which was the case in the primitive times. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) <hi type="italic">Believing in the heart that God raised him from the dead.</hi> The profession of faith with the mouth, if there be not the power of it in the heart, is but a mockery; the root of it must be laid in an unfeigned assent to the revelation of the gospel concerning Christ, especially concerning his resurrection, which is the fundamental article of the Christian faith, for thereby he was declared to be the Son of God with power, and full evidence was given that God accepted his satisfaction. <div eID="gen30748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30749" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> This is further illustrated (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.10">v. 10</reference>), and the order inverted, because there must first be faith in the heart before there can be an acceptable confession with the mouth. (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) Concerning faith: It is <hi type="italic">with the heart that man believeth,</hi> which implies more than an assent of the understanding, and takes in the consent of the will, an inward, hearty, sincere, and strong consent. It is not believing (not to be reckoned so) if it be not with the heart. This is <hi type="italic">unto righteousness.</hi> There is the righteousness of justification and the righteousness of sanctification. Faith is to both; it is the condition of our justification (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.1">ch. v. 1</reference>), and it is the root and spring of our sanctification; in it it is begun; by it it is carried on, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.9">Acts xv. 9</reference>. (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) Concerning profession: It is with <hi type="italic">the mouth that confession is made</hi>—confession to God in prayer and praise (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.6">ch. xv. 6</reference>), confession to men by owning the ways of God before others, especially when we are called to it in a day of persecution. It is fit that God should be honoured with the mouth, for he made man's mouth (<reference osisRef="Exod.4.11">Exod. iv. 11</reference>), and at such a time has promised to give his faithful people a <hi type="italic">mouth and wisdom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.21.15">Luke xxi. 15</reference>. It is part of the honour of Christ that every tongue shall confess, <reference osisRef="Phil.2.11">Phil. ii. 11</reference>. And this is said to be <hi type="italic">unto salvation,</hi> because it is the performance of the condition of that promise, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.32">Matt. x. 32</reference>. Justification by faith lays the foundation of our title to salvation; but by confession we build upon that foundation, and come at last to the full possession of that to which we were entitled. So that we have here a brief summary of the terms of salvation, and they are very reasonable; in short this, that we must devote, dedicate, and give up, to God, our souls and our bodies—our souls in believing with the heart, and our bodies in confessing with the mouth. This do, and thou shalt live. For this (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.11">v. 11</reference>) he quotes <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Isa. xxviii. 16</reference>, <hi type="italic">Whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ou kataischynthesetai.</hi></hi> That is, [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] He will not be ashamed to own that Christ in whom he trusts; he that believes in the heart will not be ashamed to confess with the mouth. It is sinful shame that makes people deny Christ, <reference osisRef="Mark.8.38">Mark viii. 38</reference>. He that believeth will not make haste (so the prophet has it)—will not make haste to run away from the sufferings he meets with in the way of his duty, will not be ashamed of a despised religion. [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] He shall not be ashamed of his hope in Christ; he shall not be disappointed of his end. It is our duty that we must not, it is our privilege that we shall not, be ashamed of our faith in Christ. He shall never have cause to repent his confidence in reposing such a trust in the Lord Jesus.
entries.2dbf33f0d7aa25b9cd7011f6ba2feffe9fdda1b3: <div eID="gen30749" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Importance of Preaching the Gospel; Perverseness of Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 58.)</title> <div sID="gen30750" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> For there is no difference between the Jew and the Greek: for the same Lord over all is rich unto all that call upon him. <hi type="super">13</hi> For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. <hi type="super">14</hi> How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? <hi type="super">15</hi> And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things! <hi type="super">16</hi> But they have not all obeyed the gospel. For Esaias saith, Lord, who hath believed our report? <hi type="super">17</hi> So then faith <hi type="italic">cometh</hi> by hearing, and hearing by the word of God. <hi type="super">18</hi> But I say, Have they not heard? Yes verily, their sound went into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world. <hi type="super">19</hi> But I say, Did not Israel know? First Moses saith, I will provoke you to jealousy by <hi type="italic">them that are</hi> no people, <hi type="italic">and</hi> by a foolish nation I will anger you. <hi type="super">20</hi> But Esaias is very bold, and saith, I was found of them that sought me not; I was made manifest unto them that asked not after me. <hi type="super">21</hi> But to Israel he saith, All day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people. <div eID="gen30750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30751" type="x-p"/> The first words express the design of the apostle through these verses, that there is no difference between Jews and Gentiles, but they stand upon the same level in point of acceptance with God. In Jesus Christ there is neither Greek nor Jews, <reference osisRef="Col.3.11">Col. iii. 11</reference>. God doth not save any nor reject any because they are Jews, nor because they are Greeks, but doth equally accept both upon gospel terms: <hi type="italic">There is no difference.</hi> For the proof of this he urges two arguments:— <div eID="gen30751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30752" type="x-p"/> I. That God is the same to all: <hi type="italic">The same Lord over all is rich unto all.</hi> There is not one God to the Jews who is more kind, and another to the Gentiles who is less kind; but he is the same to all, a common father to all mankind. When he proclaimed his name, <hi type="italic">The Lord, the Lord god, gracious and merciful,</hi> he thereby signified not only what he was to the Jews, but what he is and will be to all his creatures that seek unto him: not only good, but rich, plenteous in goodness: he hath wherewith to supply them all, and he is free and ready to give out to them; he is both able and willing: not only rich, but rich unto us, liberal and bountiful in dispensing his favours <hi type="italic">to all that call upon him.</hi> Something must be done by us, that we may reap of this bounty; and it is as little as can be, we must call upon him. He will for this be enquired of (<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.37">Ezek. xxxvi. 37</reference>), and surely that which is not worth the asking is not worth the having. We have nothing to do but to draw out by prayer, as there is occasion. <div eID="gen30752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30753" type="x-p"/> II. That the promise is the same to all (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Whoever shall call</hi>—one as well as another, without exception. This extent, this undifferencing extent, of the promise both to Jews and Gentiles he thinks should not be surprising, for it was foretold by the prophet, <reference osisRef="Joel.2.32">Joel ii. 32</reference>. Calling upon the name of the Lord is here put for all practical religion. What is the life of a Christian but a life of prayer? It implies a sense of our dependence on him, an entire dedication of ourselves to him, and a believing expectation of our all from him. He that thus calls upon him shall be saved. It is but ask and have; what would we have more? for the further illustration of this he observes, <div eID="gen30753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30754" type="x-p"/> 1. How necessary it was that the gospel should be preached to the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.14-Rom.10.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. This was what the Jews were so angry with Paul for, that he was the apostle of the Gentiles, and preached the gospel to them. Now he shows how needful it was to bring them within the reach of the forementioned promise, an interest in which they should not envy to any of their fellow-creatures. (1.) <hi type="italic">They cannot call on him in whom they have not believed.</hi> Except they believe that he is God, they will not call upon him by prayer; to what purpose should they? The grace of faith is absolutely necessary to the duty of prayer; we cannot pray aright, nor pray to acceptation, without it. He that comes to God by prayer must believe, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.6">Heb. xi. 6</reference>. Till they believed the true God, they were calling upon idols, O Baal, hear us. (2.) <hi type="italic">They cannot believe in him of whom they have not heard.</hi> some way or other the divine revelation must be made known to us, before we can receive it and assent to it; it is not born with us. In hearing is included reading, which is tantamount, and by which many are brought to believe (<reference osisRef="John.20.31">John xx. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">These things are written that you may believe.</hi> But hearing only is mentioned, as the more ordinary and natural way of receiving information. (3.) <hi type="italic">They cannot hear without a preacher;</hi> how should they? Somebody must tell them what they are to believe. Preachers and hearers are correlates; it is a blessed thing when they mutually rejoice in each other—the hearers in the skill and faithfulness of the preacher, and the preacher in the willingness and obedience of the hearers. (4.) <hi type="italic">They cannot preach except they be sent,</hi> except they be both commissioned and in some measure qualified for their preaching work. How shall a man act as an ambassador, unless he have both his credentials and his instructions from the prince that sends him? This proves that to the regular ministry there must be a regular mission and ordination. It is God's prerogative to send ministers; he is the Lord of the harvest, and therefore to him we must <hi type="italic">pray that he would send forth labourers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.9.38">Matt. ix. 38</reference>. He only can qualify men for, and incline them to, the work of the ministry. But the competency of that qualification, and the sincerity of that inclination, must not be left to the judgment of every man for himself: the nature of the thing will by no means admit this; but, for the preservation of due order in the church, this must needs be referred and submitted to the judgment of a competent number of those who are themselves in that office and of approved wisdom and experience in it, who, as in all other callings, are presumed the most able judges, and who are empowered to set apart such as they find so qualified and inclined to this work of the ministry, that by this preservation of the succession the name of Christ may endure for ever and his throne as the days of heaven. And those that are thus set apart, not only may, but must preach, as those that are sent. <div eID="gen30754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30755" type="x-p"/> 2. How welcome the gospel ought to be to those to whom it was preached, because it showed the way to salvation, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.15">v. 15</reference>. For this he quotes <reference osisRef="Isa.52.7">Isa. lii. 7</reference>. The like passage we have, <reference osisRef="Nah.1.15">Nah. i. 15</reference>, which, if it point at the glad tidings of the deliverance of Israel out of Babylon in the type, yet looks further to the gospel, the good news of our salvation by Jesus Christ. Observe, (1.) What the gospel is: It is <hi type="italic">the gospel of peace;</hi> it is the word of reconciliation between God and man. <hi type="italic">On earth peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.2.14">Luke ii. 14</reference>. Or, peace is put in general for all good; so it is explained here; it is <hi type="italic">glad tidings of good things.</hi> The things of the gospel are good things indeed, the best things; tidings concerning them are the most joyful tidings, the best news that ever came from heaven to earth. (2.) What the work of ministers is: To preach this gospel, to <hi type="italic">bring these glad tidings;</hi> to <hi type="italic">evangelize peace</hi> (so the original is), to evangelize good things. Every good preacher is in this sense an evangelist: he is not only a messenger to carry the news, but an ambassador to treat; and the first gospel preachers were angels, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.13">Luke ii. 13</reference>, &c. (3.) How acceptable they should therefore be to the children of men for their work's sake: <hi type="italic">How beautiful are the feet,</hi> that is, how welcome are they! Mary Magdalene expressed her love to Christ by kissing his feet, and afterwards by holding him by the feet, <reference osisRef="Matt.28.9">Matt. xxviii. 9</reference>. And, when Christ was sending forth his disciples, he washed their feet. Those that preach the gospel of peace should see to it that their feet (their life and conversation) be beautiful: the holiness of ministers' lives is the beauty of their feet. <hi type="italic">How beautiful!</hi> namely, in the eyes of those that hear them. Those that welcome the message cannot but love the messengers. See <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.12-1Thess.5.13">1 Thess. v. 12, 13</reference>. <div eID="gen30755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30756" type="x-p"/> 3. He answers an objection against all this, which might be taken from the little success which the gospel had in many places (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">But they have not all obeyed the gospel.</hi> All the Jews have not, all the Gentiles have not; far the greater part of both remain in unbelief and disobedience. Observe, The gospel is given us not only to be known and believed, but to be obeyed. It is not a system of notions, but a rule of practice. This little success of the word was likewise foretold by the prophet (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.1">Isa. liii. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Who hath believed our report?</hi> Very few have, few to what one would think should have believed it, considering how faithful a report it is and how well worthy of all acceptation,—very few to the many that persist in unbelief. It is no strange thing, but it is a very sad and uncomfortable thing, for the ministers of Christ to bring the report of the gospel, and not to be believed in it. Under such a melancholy consideration it is good for us to go to God and make our complaint to him. <hi type="italic">Lord, who hath believed,</hi> &c. In answer to this, <div eID="gen30756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30757" type="x-p"/> (1.) He shows that the word preached is the ordinary means of working faith (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">So then,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ara</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">however;</hi> though many that hear do not believe, yet those that believe have first heard. <hi type="italic">Faith cometh by hearing.</hi> It is the summary of what he had said before, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.14">v. 14</reference>. The beginning, progress, and strength of faith, are by hearing. The word of God is therefore called <hi type="italic">the word of faith:</hi> it begets and nourishes faith. God gives faith, but it is by the word as the instrument. <hi type="italic">Hearing</hi> (that hearing which works faith) is <hi type="italic">by the word of God.</hi> It is not hearing the enticing words of man's wisdom, but hearing the word of God, that will befriend faith, and hearing it as the word of God. See <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.13">1 Thess. ii. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen30757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30758" type="x-p"/> (2.) That those who would not believe the report of the gospel, yet, having heard it, were thereby left inexcusable, and may thank themselves for their own ruin, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.18">v. 18</reference>, <hi type="italic">to the end.</hi> <div eID="gen30758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30759" type="x-p"/> [1.] The Gentiles have heard it (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">Have they not heard?</hi> Yes, more or less, they have either heard the gospel, or at least heard of it. <hi type="italic">Their sound went into all the earth;</hi> not only a confused sound, but their <hi type="italic">words</hi> (more distinct and intelligible notices of these things) are <hi type="italic">gone unto the ends of the world.</hi> The commission which the apostles received runs thus: <hi type="italic">Go you into all the world—preach to every creature—disciple all nations;</hi> and they did with indefatigable industry and wonderful success pursue that commission. See the extent of Paul's province, <reference osisRef="Rom.15.19">ch. xv. 19</reference>. To this remote island of Britain, one of the utmost corners of the world, not only the sound, but the words, of the gospel came within a few years after Christ's ascension. It was in order to this that the gift of tongues was at the very first poured so plentifully upon the apostles, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.1-Acts.2.47">Acts ii</reference>. In the expression here he plainly alludes to <reference osisRef="Ps.19.4">Ps. xix. 4</reference>, which speaks of the notices which the visible works of God in the creation give to all the world of the power and Godhead of the Creator. As under the Old Testament God provided for the publishing of the work of creation by the sun, moon, and stars, so now for the publishing of the work of redemption to all the world by the preaching of gospel ministers, who are therefore called <hi type="italic">stars.</hi> <div eID="gen30759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30760" type="x-p"/> [2.] The Jews have heard it too, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.19-Rom.10.21">v. 19-21</reference>. For this he appeals to two passages of the Old Testament, to show how inexcusable they are too. <hi type="italic">Did not Israel know</hi> that the Gentiles were to be called in? They might have known it from Moses and Isaiah. <div eID="gen30760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30761" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> One is taken from <reference osisRef="Deut.32.21">Deut. xxxii. 21</reference>, <hi type="italic">I will provoke you to jealousy.</hi> The Jews not only had the offer, but saw the Gentiles accepting it and benefitted by that acceptance, witness their vexation at the event. They had the refusal: <hi type="italic">To you first,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.3.26">Acts iii. 26</reference>. In all places where the apostles came still the Jews had the first offer, and the Gentiles had but their leavings. If one would not, another would. Now this provoked them to jealousy. They, as the elder brother in the parable (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.1-Luke.15.32">Luke xv.</reference>) envied the reception and entertainment of the prodigal Gentiles upon their repentance. The Gentiles are here called <hi type="italic">no people,</hi> and <hi type="italic">a foolish nation,</hi> that is, not the professing people of God. How much soever there be of the wit and wisdom of the world, those that are not the people of God are, and in the end will be found to be, a foolish people. Such was the state of the Gentile world, who yet were made the people of God, and Christ to them the wisdom of God. What a provocation it was to the Jews to see the Gentiles taken into favour we may see, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.45">Acts xiii. 45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.17.5 Acts.17.13">xvii. 5, 13</reference>, and especially <reference osisRef="Acts.22.22">Acts xxii. 22</reference>. It was an instance of the great wickedness of the Jews that they were thus enraged; and this in Deuteronomy is the matter of a threatening. God often makes people's sin their punishment. A man needs no greater plague than to be left to the impetuous rage of his own lusts. <div eID="gen30761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30762" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Another is taken from <reference osisRef="Isa.65.1-Isa.65.2">Isa. lxv. 1, 2</reference>, which is very full, and in it Esaias is very bold—bold indeed, to speak so plainly of the rejection of his own countrymen. Those that will be found faithful have need to be very bold. Those that are resolved to please God must not be afraid to displease any man. Now Esaias speaks boldly and plainly, <div eID="gen30762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30763" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> Of the preventing grace and favour of God in the reception and entertainment of the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">I was found of those that sought me not.</hi> The prescribed method is, Seek and find; this is a rule for us, not a rule for God, who is often found of those that do not seek. His grace is his own, distinguishing grace his own, and he dispenses it in a way of sovereignty, gives of withholds it at pleasure—anticipates us with the blessings, the riches choicest blessings, of his goodness. Thus he manifested himself to the Gentiles, by sending the light of the gospel among them, when they were so far from seeking him and asking after him that they were following after lying vanities, and serving dumb idols. Was not this our own particular case? Did not God begin in love, and manifest himself to us when we did not ask after him? And was not that a time of love indeed, to be often remembered with a great deal of thankfulness? <div eID="gen30763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30764" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> Of the obstinacy and perverseness of Israel, notwithstanding the fair offers and affectionate invitations they had, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.21">v. 21</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen30764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30765" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) God's great goodness to them: <hi type="italic">All day long I have stretched forth my hands.</hi> [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] His offers: <hi type="italic">I have stretched forth my hands,</hi> offering them life and salvation with the greatest sincerity and seriousness that can be, with all possible expressions of earnestness and importunity, showing them the happiness tendered, setting it before them with the greatest evidence, reasoning the case with them. Stretching forth the hands is the gesture of those that require audience (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.1">Acts xxvi. 1</reference>), or desire acceptance, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.24">Prov. i. 24</reference>. Christ was crucified with his hands stretched out. <hi type="italic">Stretched forth my hands</hi> as offering reconciliation—come let us shake hands and be friends; and our duty is to give the hand to him, <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.8">2 Chron. xxx. 8</reference>. [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] His patience in making these offers: <hi type="italic">All day long.</hi> The patience of God towards provoking sinners is admirable. He waits to be gracious. The time of God's patience is here called a day, lightsome as a day and fit for work and business, but limited as a day, and a night at the end of it. he bears long, but he will not bear always. <div eID="gen30765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30766" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) Their great badness to him. They were a <hi type="italic">disobedient gainsaying people.</hi> One word in the Hebrew, in Isaiah, is here well explained by two; not only disobedient to the call, not yielding to it, but gainsaying, and quarrelling with it, which is much worse. Many that will not accept of a good proposal will yet acknowledge that they have nothing to say against it: but the Jews who believed not rested not there, but contradicted and blasphemed. God's patience with them was a very great aggravation of their disobedience, and rendered it the more exceedingly sinful; as their disobedience advanced the honour of God's patience and rendered it the more exceedingly gracious. It is a wonder of mercy in God that his goodness is not overcome by man's badness; and it is a wonder of wickedness in man that his badness is not overcome by God's goodness.  <chapter eID="Rom.10"/> <div eID="gen30766" type="x-p"/>

Same Subject Continued--How Israel Came to Miss Salvation, and the Gentiles to Find It.</title> <div sID="gen32356" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16565"/><hi type="bold">1. Brethren, my heart's desire--</hi>The word here expresses "entire complacency," that in which the heart would experience full satisfaction.<div eID="gen32356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32357" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and prayer--</hi>"supplication."<div eID="gen32357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32358" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to God for Israel--</hi>"for them" is the true reading; the subject being continued from the close of the preceding chapter.<div eID="gen32358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32359" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is, that they may be saved--</hi>"for their salvation." Having before poured forth the anguish of his soul at the general unbelief of his nation and its dreadful consequences (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.1-Rom.9.3">Ro 9:1-3</reference>), he here expresses in the most emphatic terms his desire and prayer for their salvation. <div eID="gen32359" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c970a5fb3a4ecead052b594ffff96a0301a212f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16566"/><div sID="gen32360" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16566"/><hi type="bold">2. For I bear them record--</hi>or, "witness," as he well could from his own sad experience.<div eID="gen32360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32361" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that they have a zeal of--</hi>"for"<div eID="gen32361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32362" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God, but not according to knowledge--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Acts.22.3">Ac 22:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.26.9-Acts.26.11">26:9-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.1.13">Ga 1:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.14">14</reference>). He alludes to this well-meaning of his people, notwithstanding their spiritual blindness, not certainly to excuse their rejection of Christ and rage against His saints, but as some ground of hope regarding them. (See <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.13">1Ti 1:13</reference>). <div eID="gen32362" type="x-p"/>

For they being ignorant of God's righteousness--</hi>that is, for the justification of the guilty (see on <reference osisRef="Rom.1.17">Ro 1:17</reference>).<div eID="gen32363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32364" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and going about--</hi>"seeking"<div eID="gen32364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32365" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves to the righteousness of God--</hi>The apostle views the general rejection of Christ by the nation as one act. <div eID="gen32365" type="x-p"/>
entries.235a63926495a5e37366627d7b175b396559b0a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16568"/><div sID="gen32366" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16568"/><hi type="bold">4. For Christ is the end--</hi>the object or aim.<div eID="gen32366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32367" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the law for--</hi>justifying<div eID="gen32367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32368" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness to every one that believeth--</hi>that is, contains within Himself all that the law demands for the justification of such as embrace Him, whether Jew or Gentile (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.24">Ga 3:24</reference>). <div eID="gen32368" type="x-p"/>
entries.e8c85e5654376639ef067af474f4687d60dec5fe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16569"/><div sID="gen32369" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16569"/><hi type="bold">5-10. For Moses describeth the righteousness which is of the law, That the man that doeth--</hi>"hath done"<div eID="gen32369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32370" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">those things--</hi>which it commands.<div eID="gen32370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32371" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall live in them--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Lev.18.5">Le 18:5</reference>). This is the one way of justification and life--by "the righteousness which is of (or, by our own obedience to) the law." <div eID="gen32371" type="x-p"/>
entries.8badc7878cc9642756eeb2f28085ed4c6ff0164b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16575"/><div sID="gen32387" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16575"/><hi type="bold">11-13. For the scripture saith--</hi>in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Is 28:16</reference>, a glorious Messianic passage.<div eID="gen32387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32388" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed--</hi>Here, as in <reference osisRef="Rom.9.33">Ro 9:33</reference>, the quotation is from the Septuagint, which renders those words of the original, "shall not make haste" (that is, fly for escape, as from conscious danger), "shall not be put to shame," which comes to the same thing. <div eID="gen32388" type="x-p"/>
entries.eae809c5538ca86524f9aed37fe8d61903c36e5d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16578"/><div sID="gen32396" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16578"/>14-15. How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? <hi type="bold">and ... believe in him of whom they have not heard? and ... hear without a preacher? and ... preach except ... sent?--</hi>that is, "True, the same Lord over all is rich unto all alike that call upon Him. But this calling implies believing, and believing hearing, and hearing preaching, and preaching a mission to preach: Why, then, take ye it so ill, O children of Abraham, that in obedience to our heavenly mission (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.16-Acts.26.18">Ac 26:16-18</reference>) we preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ?" <div eID="gen32396" type="x-p"/>
entries.4935d423049e83767e46fd98d00ad991409b1ff3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16580"/><div sID="gen32399" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16580"/><hi type="bold">16-17. But they have not all obeyed the gospel--</hi>that is, the Scripture hath prepared us to expect this sad result.<div eID="gen32399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32400" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">For Esaias saith, Lord, who hath believed our report?--</hi>that is,"Where shall one find a believer?" The prophet speaks as if next to none would believe: The apostle softens this into "They have not all believed." <div eID="gen32400" type="x-p"/>
entries.f9a7a5195a86490ec8413d0a6ec166852ab81670: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16582"/><div sID="gen32402" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16582"/><hi type="bold">18. But I say, Have they not heard?--</hi>"Did they not hear?" Can Israel, through any region of his dispersion, plead ignorance of these glad tidings?<div eID="gen32402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32403" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Yes, verily, their sound went--</hi>"their voice went out"<div eID="gen32403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32404" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into all the earth, and their words unto the end of the world--</hi>These beautiful words are from <reference osisRef="Ps.19.4">Psa 19:4</reference>. Whether the apostle quoted them as in their primary intention applicable to his subject (as Olshausen, Alford, &c.), or only "used scriptural language to express his own ideas, as is done involuntarily almost by every preacher in every sermon" [Hodge], expositors are not agreed. But though the latter may seem the more natural since "the rising of the Sun of righteousness upon the world" (Mal 4:2), "the Dayspring from on high visiting us, giving light to them that sat in darkness, and guiding our feet into the way of peace" (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.78">Lu 1:78</reference>, 79), must have been familiar and delightful to the apostle's ear, we cannot doubt that the irradiation of the world with the beams of a better Sun by the universal diffusion of the Gospel of Christ, must have a mode of speaking quite natural, and to him scarcely figurative. <div eID="gen32404" type="x-p"/>
entries.4d7e227543df2dd16ec8041e140eae8868983188: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16583"/><div sID="gen32405" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16583"/><hi type="bold">19. But I say, Did not Israel know?--</hi>know, from their own Scriptures, of God's intention to bring in the Gentiles?<div eID="gen32405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32406" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">First--</hi>that is First in the prophetic line [De Wette].<div eID="gen32406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32407" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Moses saith, &c.--</hi>"I will provoke you to jealousy ('against') [them that are] not a nation, and against a nation without understanding will I anger you" (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.21">De 32:21</reference>). In this verse God warns His ancient people that because they had (that is, in aftertimes would) moved Him to jealousy with their "no-gods," and provoked Him to anger with their vanities, He in requital would move them to jealousy by receiving into His favor a "no-people," and provoke them to anger by adopting a nation void of understanding. <div eID="gen32407" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f11c913b2a668965fe9b3672cf85c4c7fa585d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16584"/><div sID="gen32408" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16584"/><hi type="bold">20. But Esaias is very bold, and saith--</hi>that is, is still plainer, and goes even the length of saying.<div eID="gen32408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32409" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I was found of them that sought me not--</hi>until I sought them.<div eID="gen32409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32410" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I was made--</hi>"became"<div eID="gen32410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32411" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">manifest unto them that asked not after me--</hi>until the invitation from Me came to them. That the calling of the Gentiles was meant by these words of the prophet (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.1">Is 65:1</reference>) is manifest from what immediately follows, "I said, Behold Me, behold Me, unto a nation that was not called by My name." <div eID="gen32411" type="x-p"/>
entries.81c2c5c308cf4362e8a1e96e5db5a18f6a872667: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16585"/><div sID="gen32412" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16585"/><hi type="bold">21. But to--</hi>rather, "with regard to"<div eID="gen32412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32413" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Israel he saith, All day--</hi>"All the day"<div eID="gen32413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32414" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">long I have stretched out my hands--</hi>"did I stretch forth"<div eID="gen32414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32415" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my hands--</hi>the attitude of gracious entreaty.<div eID="gen32415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32416" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto a disobedient and gainsaying people--</hi>These words, which immediately follow the announcement just quoted of the calling of the Gentiles, were enough to forewarn the Jews both of God's purpose to eject them from their privileges, in favor of the Gentiles, and of the cause of it on their own part.<div eID="gen32416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32417" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Note, (1) Mere sincerity, and even earnestness in religion--</hi>though it may be some ground of hope for a merciful recovery from error--is no excuse, and will not compensate, for the deliberate rejection of saving truth, when in the providence of God presented for acceptance (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.1-Rom.10.3">Ro 10:1-3</reference>; and see on <reference osisRef="Rom.9.7">Ro 9:7</reference>, Note 7). (2) The true cause of such rejection of saving truth, by the otherwise sincere, is the prepossession of the mind by some false notions of its own. So long as the Jews "sought to set up their own righteousness," it was in the nature of things impossible that they should "submit themselves to the righteousness of God"; the one of these two methods of acceptance being in the teeth of the other (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.3">Ro 10:3</reference>). (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.3">3</reference>) The essential terms of salvation have in every age been the same: "Whosoever will" is invited to "take of the water of life freely," <reference osisRef="Rev.22.17">Re 22:17</reference> (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.13">Ro 10:13</reference>). (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.4">4</reference>) How will the remembrance of the simplicity, reasonableness, and absolute freeness of God's plan of salvation overwhelm those that perish from under the sound of it (Ro 10:4-13). (5) How piercingly and perpetually should that question--"How shall they hear without a preacher?"--sound in the ears of all churches, as but the apostolic echo of their Lord's parting injunction, "Preach the Gospel to every creature" (<reference osisRef="Mark.16.15">Mr 16:15</reference>), and how far below the proper standard of love, zeal, and self-sacrifice must the churches as yet be, when with so plenteous a harvest the laborers are yet so few (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.37">Mt 9:37</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.38">38</reference>), and that cry from the lips of pardoned, gifted, consecrated men--"Here am I, send me" (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.8">Is 6:8</reference>), is not heard everywhere (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.14">Ro 10:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.15">15</reference>)! (6) The blessing of a covenant relation to God is the irrevocable privilege of no people and no Church; it can be preserved only by fidelity, on our part, to the covenant itself (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.19">Ro 10:19</reference>). (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.7">7</reference>) God is often found by those who apparently are the farthest from Him, while He remains undiscovered by those who think themselves the nearest (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.20">Ro 10:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.21">21</reference>). (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.8">8</reference>) God's dealings even with reprobate sinners are full of tenderness and compassion; all the day long extending the arms of His mercy even to the disobedient and gainsaying. This will be felt and acknowledged at last by all who perish, to the glory of God's forbearance and to their own confusion (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.21">Ro 10:21</reference>). <chapter eID="Rom.10"/>

entries.9f63580609059b39ef674e4e0b99216add3a126d: <div eID="gen46749" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen46750" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen46751" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen46751" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen46750" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen46752" type="x-p"/> The apostle expresses his earnest desire for the salvation of the Jews, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.1">Rom 10:1</reference>. Having a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, they sought salvation by works, and not by faith in Christ, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.2-Rom.10.4">Rom 10:2-4</reference>. The righteousness which is of the law described, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.5">Rom 10:5</reference>. That which is by faith described also, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.6-Rom.10.10">Rom 10:6-10</reference>. He that believes and calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.11-Rom.10.13">Rom 10:11-13</reference>. What is necessary to salvation, believing, hearing, preaching, a Divine mission, the Gospel, and obedience to its precepts, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.14-Rom.10.16">Rom 10:14-16</reference>. Faith comes by hearing, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.17">Rom 10:17</reference>. The universal spread of the Gospel predicted by the prophets, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.18-Rom.10.20">Rom 10:18-20</reference>. The ingratitude and disobedience of the Israelites, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.21">Rom 10:21</reference>. <div eID="gen46752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46753" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen46753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46754" type="x-p"/> My heart's desire, etc. - Though the apostle knew that the Jews were now in a state of rejection, yet he knew also that they were in this state through their own obstinacy, and that God was still waiting to be gracious, and consequently, that they might still repent and turn to him. Of his concern for their salvation he had already given ample proof, when he was willing to become a sacrifice for their welfare, see <reference osisRef="Rom.9.3">Rom 9:3</reference>.
entries.1312dc3df62568a5d1a4d71a7128a31dde9970e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen46754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46755" type="x-p"/> They have a zeal of God - They believe their law to have come immediately from God himself, and are jealous of its glory and excellence; they conscientiously observe its rites and ceremonies, but they do not consider the object and end of those rites; they sin more through ignorance than malice; and this pleads in their excuse. By this fine apology for them, the apostle prepares them for the harsher truths which he was about to deliver.
entries.21284bfb452f0f2e225fedca21a2d38c419017b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen46755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46756" type="x-p"/> For - being ignorant of God's righteousness - Not knowing God's method of saving sinners, which is the only proper and efficient method: and going about to establish their own righteousness - seeking to procure their salvation by means of their own contriving; they have not submitted - they have not bowed to the determinations of the Most High, relative to his mode of saving mankind, viz. through faith in Jesus Christ, as the only available sacrifice for sin - the end to which the law pointed.
entries.c703bfd3a9ccd4b0fd3ea80d8aad44ccfeecc657: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen46756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46757" type="x-p"/> For Christ is the end of the law - Where the law ends, Christ begins. The law ends with representative sacrifices; Christ begins with the real offering. The law is our schoolmaster to lead us to Christ; it cannot save, but it leaves us at his door, where alone salvation is to be found. Christ as an atoning sacrifice for sin, was the grand object of the whole sacrificial code of Moses; his passion and death were the fulfillment of its great object and design. Separate this sacrificial death of Christ from the law, and the law has no meaning, for it is impossible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sins: wherefore the Messiah is represented as saying, Sacrifice and observing thou didst not desire; burnt-offering and sin-offering thou hast not required; then said I, Lo, I come to do thy will; a body hast thou prepared me, <reference osisRef="Psa.40.6">Psa 40:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.40.7">Psa 40:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.4-Heb.10.10">Heb 10:4-10</reference>; which proves that God never designed that the sacrifices of the law should be considered the atonement for sin, but a type or representative of that atonement; and that The atonement was the sacrifice offered by Christ. Thus he was the End of the law, in respect to its sacrifices. And, as sacrifices were offered merely to procure pardon of sin, righteousness, or justification, Christ is the end of the law for this justification to every one that believeth on him, as dying for their offenses, and rising again for their justification, having made peace through the blood of his cross. Therefore every Jew who rejected Christ rejected salvation, and that very salvation which the law witnessed and required, and which could not be had but through Christ alone.
entries.a1d39dada04d504583dd1e54ddeba8b212064c5e: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen46757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46758" type="x-p"/> For Moses describeth the righteousness which is of the law - The place to which the apostle refers, seems to be <reference osisRef="Lev.18.5">Lev 18:5</reference> : Ye shall therefore keep my statutes and my judgments; which if a man do, he shall live in them. These words seem to be spoken in answer to an objection which might be made by a Jew: "Did not Moses give us a law, the observance of which should secure our salvation?" Such a law Moses undoubtedly gave, and that law promises life to those who perform its precepts: but who can plead for life on this ground, who rejects that Christ who is the end of the law? No man ever did, nor ever can, fulfill that law, so as to merit salvation by the performance of it: for, as all have sinned and come short of the glory of God, they are all under the curse of the law, which says: Cursed is every one who continueth not in all the things that are written in the book of the law to do them, <reference osisRef="Deu.27.26">Deu 27:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.10">Gal 3:10</reference>; therefore by the deeds of this law none can be justified, because all are in a state of condemnation for transgressions already committed against it. If, therefore, there were not such a provision as is made by the death of Christ, no soul could be saved.
entries.9b203281c986ae2bf99cce85dfcd0b9fcdfb7d8d: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen46758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46759" type="x-p"/> But the righteousness which is of faith - As it is most evident that there can be no justification by works, as all are sinful and all in a guilty state; if God will grant salvation at all, it must be by faith: but faith must have an object and a reason for its exercise; the object is Jesus Christ - the reason is the infinite merit of his passion and death. <div eID="gen46759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46760" type="x-p"/> Who shall ascend unto heaven? etc. - As Christ is the end of the law for justification to every one that believes, no observance of the law can procure him. Who, by the practice of the law, can bring Christ down from heaven? or, when brought down, and crucified and buried, as a sacrifice for sin, who can bring him up again from the dead? And both his death and resurrection are essentially necessary for the salvation of a lost world. Or the sense of the apostle may be this: They who will not believe in Christ crucified must in effect be seeking another Messiah to come down from heaven with a different revelation; or they who will not credit the doctrine that we preach concerning his resurrection seem in effect to say, Christ yet remains to be raised from the dead, and reign over the Jews as a mighty secular sovereign, subjecting the Gentile world to the sway of his righteous scepter.
entries.19c0023c1a66e8bb70ec31305df7420a6de25875: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen46760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46761" type="x-p"/> But what saith it? The word is nigh thee - There is no occasion to seek high or low for the saving power; the word of reconciliation is nigh. The way of salvation is now both plain and easy. The law is magnified and made honorable by the death of Christ; and the doctrine of faith in his death and resurrection is fully proclaimed, and amply proved to be effectual to the purpose for which it was revealed. By the preaching of the Gospel the doctrine of salvation is nigh thee, and the saving influence is at hand: it is in thy mouth, easy to be understood, easy to be professed: and in thy heart, if thou art upright before God, sincerely desiring to be saved on his own terms, not striving to establish thy own method of justification by the law, which must for ever be ineffectual, but submitting to the method of justification which God has devised.
entries.b55ba8fb25cd818cfc1bf66377dc76c8d0275882: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen46761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46762" type="x-p"/> That if thou shalt confess, etc. - Acknowledge the Lord Jesus Christ as the only Savior. Believe in thy heart that he who died for thy offenses has been raised for thy justification; and depend solely on him for that justification, and thou shalt be saved.
entries.45f9528c735748c3a5ca280d2e9b714d308b2e57: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen46762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46763" type="x-p"/> For with the heart man believeth, etc. - And be sincere in this: for with the heart, duly affected with a sense of guilt, and of the sufficiency of the sacrifice which Christ has offered, man believeth unto righteousness, believeth to receive justification; for this is the proper meaning of the term here, and in many other parts of this epistle; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. He who believes aright in Christ Jesus will receive such a full conviction of the truth, and such an evidence of his redemption, that his mouth will boldly confess his obligation to his Redeemer, and the blessed persuasion he has of the remission of all his sins through the blood of the cross. One grand object of the apostle is to show the simplicity of the Gospel scheme of salvation; and at the same time, its great efficacy, it is simple, and very unlike the law, which was full of rites, ordinances, ceremonies, etc., each of which required to be perfectly fulfilled: and yet, after all, even those who had the utmost zeal for God, and, as conscientiously as possible, observed all the precepts of the law, had not attained to justification nor peace of conscience. Whereas both Jews and Gentiles, who had believed on the Lord Jesus according to the simple declarations of the Gospel, were freely justified from all things from which they could not be justified by the law of Moses: and they had the witness in themselves that they were passed from death to life.
entries.d732392edf63deebb4407dc1e331641b22d9ab28: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen46763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46764" type="x-p"/> For the Scripture saith - And howsoever the Jews may despise this Gospel, because it comes not unto them with pomp and ceremony, it puts those who receive it into possession of every heavenly blessing: and this is according to the positive declarations of the prophets; for it is written, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Isa 28:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.23">Isa 49:23</reference> : Whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed. He shall neither be disappointed of his hope, nor ashamed of his confidence; because he has that faith which is the evidence of things not seen, the subsistence of things hoped for, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.1">Heb 11:1</reference>. See note on <reference osisRef="Rom.1.16">Rom 1:16</reference>.
entries.364a3878f73e3f59bcbf4dcff6049f8b0c301bed: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen46764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46765" type="x-p"/> For there is no difference between the Jew and the Greek - All are equally welcome to this salvation. Here the Jew has no exclusive privilege; and from this the Greek is not rejected. One simple way of being saved is proposed to all, viz. faith in the Lord Jesus Christ; because he is the same Lord who has made all and governs all, and is rich in mercy to all that call upon him.
entries.a0952ff3424df86a861178ffc0eeea6f51f20962: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen46765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46766" type="x-p"/> For whosoever shall call, etc. - Nor shall any one who hears this doctrine of salvation, and credits it as he is commanded, be permitted to pray or supplicate the throne of grace in vain: for the Prophet Joel hath declared, <reference osisRef="Joe.2.32">Joe 2:32</reference> : Whosoever shall call upon, invoke, the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior of sinners, shall be saved - shall have his guilt pardoned, his heart purified; and if he abide in the faith, rooted and grounded in him, showing forth the virtues of him who was called him out of darkness into his marvellous light, he shall be saved with all the power of an eternal life. "Believing in Christ, or God, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.11">Rom 10:11</reference>, and calling upon God, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.12-Rom.10.14">Rom 10:12-14</reference>, are in effect the same thing; as calling upon God necessarily connects and supposes faith in him: and he who duly believes in Christ has such a sense of his dependence upon Divine grace, that he looks unto God and trusts in his power and goodness alone for happiness: which is the true religion of the Gospel." Dr. Taylor. <div eID="gen46766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46767" type="x-p"/> It is evident that St. Paul understood the text of Joel as relating to our blessed Lord; and therefore his word κυριος must answer to the prophet's word יהוה Yehovah, which is no mean proof of the Godhead of Jesus Christ. If the text be translated, Whosoever shall invoke in the name of the Lord, which translation יקרא בשם יהוה yikra beshem Yehovah will certainly bear, yet still the term Yehovah, the incommunicable name, is given to Christ; because invoking in the name signifies soliciting one in the name or on the account of another. He who is invoked is God; he, in whose name he is invoked, is Jesus Christ, who is here called Yehovah. He who asks mercy from God, in the name and for the sake of Jesus Christ, shall get his soul saved.
entries.c6a8e45c11e1b8dabb44210a504c3f999d01d173: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen46767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46768" type="x-p"/> How then shall they call on him - As the apostle had laid so much stress on believing in order to salvation, and as this doctrine, without farther explanation, might be misunderstood, it was necessary to show how this faith was produced; and therefore he lays the whole doctrine down in a beautifully graduated order. <div eID="gen46768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46769" type="x-p"/> 1. There can be no salvation without the Gospel: a dispensation of mercy and grace from God alone, here called, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.15">Rom 10:15</reference>, the Gospel of peace; glad tidings of good things. <div eID="gen46769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46770" type="x-p"/> 2. This must be preached, proclaimed in the world for the obedience of faith. <div eID="gen46770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46771" type="x-p"/> 3. None can effectually preach this unless he have a Divine mission; for how shall they preach except they be Sent, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.15">Rom 10:15</reference>. The matter must come from God; and the person mho proclaims it must have both authority and unction from on high. <div eID="gen46771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46772" type="x-p"/> 4. This Divinely-commissioned person must be heard: it is the duty of all, to whom this message of salvation is sent, to hear it with the deepest reverence and attention. <div eID="gen46772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46773" type="x-p"/> 5. What is heard must be credited; for they who do not believe the Gospel as the record which God has given of his Son cannot be saved, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.14">Rom 10:14</reference>. <div eID="gen46773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46774" type="x-p"/> 6. Those who believe must invoke God by Christ, which they cannot do unless they believe in him; and in this way alone they are to expect salvation. Professing to believe in Christ, without earnest, importunate prayer for salvation, can save no man. All these things the apostle lays down as essentially necessary; and they all follow from his grand proposition, Whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. But, says the apostle, How shall they Call upon him in whom they have not believed? And how shall they Believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they Hear without a preacher? And how shall they Preach except they be sent? And with what message which can bring salvation can they be sent, but with the Gospel of Peace, the Glad Tidings Of Good Things. When, therefore, there is: 1st, a proper Message; 2ndly, a proper Messenger; 3rdly, the message Preached, proclaimed, or properly delivered by him; 4thly, the proclamation properly Heard and attentively considered by the people; 5thly, the message which they have heard, conscientiously Believed; 6thly, the name of the Lord Jesus, by whom alone this salvation is provided, most fervently Invoked; then, 7thly, salvation, or redemption from sin and misery, and the enjoyment of peace and happiness, will be the result of such calling, believing, hearing, preaching, sending, and message sent: - and thus the doctrine of salvation by grace through faith is guarded from abuse.
entries.6e4bad7c8b827e6a7b289a8757b9482c0c1b1991: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen46774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46775" type="x-p"/> How beautiful are the feet of them that preach - Dr. Taylor remarks on this quotation, which is taken from <reference osisRef="Isa.52.7">Isa 52:7</reference>, that "feet are variously used in Scripture, and sometimes have respect to things internal and spiritual. For as the life of man and the practice of piety are compared to walking, <reference osisRef="Psa.1.1">Psa 1:1</reference>, so his feet may signify the principles on which he acts, and the dispositions of his mind. <reference osisRef="Ecc.5.1">Ecc 5:1</reference> : Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God. Agreeably to this, the feet of the messengers in Isaiah and of the apostles in this verse, may signify the validity of their mission - the authority upon which they acted, and any character or qualifications with which they were invested."
entries.9f77271958cc348126827e7dd2b796f35b0a8492: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen46775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46776" type="x-p"/> But they have not all obeyed the Gospel - This seems to be the objection of a Jew; as if he had said: A Divine mission would be attended with success; whereas there are numbers who pay no attention to the glad tidings you preach. To this the apostle answers, that the Spirit of God, by Isaiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.1">Isa 53:1</reference>, foretold it would be so, even in the case of the Jews themselves, where he said, Lord, who hath believed our report? For although God brings the message of salvation to men, he does not oblige them to embrace it. <div eID="gen46776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46777" type="x-p"/> It is proposed to their understanding and conscience; but it does not become the means of salvation unless it be affectionately credited.
entries.fb0e476c893cde3764a6c74f461cc4a7972b8d12: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen46777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46778" type="x-p"/> So then faith cometh by hearing - Preaching the Gospel is the ordinary means of salvation; faith in Christ is the result of hearing the word, the doctrine of God preached.
